question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

In CFOP PLL the U face is already oriented so the nine U stickers are all the same colour and give no permutation information at all. You have to read the U-layer pieces from their side colours.

There are 8 pieces in the U layer: 4 edges and 4 corners. An edge in the U layer shows exactly one non-U sticker on the side, and a corner shows at least one non-U sticker on the side for identification purposes. To know which piece is sitting in each of the four edge slots and which corner is sitting in each of the four corner slots you need a distinguishing side sticker for every piece.

That is one informative non-top sticker per piece, 4 for the edges and 4 for the corners, 8 in total. With the 8 side stickers you can read the headlights, the block patterns and the permutation of the four corners vs the four edges and the case is unambiguous up to AUF.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

When the last layer is oriented after OLL the U face is monochrome, so the whole permutation information is carried on the side stickers of the U slice. There are 8 distinct pieces in the U layer – 4 corners and 4 edges – and each piece is identifiable from the colour of at least one of its side stickers in the visible U row.

The four edges each contribute one unique side sticker to the front, right, back and left faces, and the four corners each contribute a unique side sticker that is visible on the same four faces. In practice you can recognise the edge permutation from the four edge side stickers and the corner permutation from the four corner side stickers, i.e. one sticker per U-layer piece. That is 4 + 4 = 8 non-U stickers that are enough to read the whole edge and corner permutation and therefore name the exact PLL case up to rotation.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is monochrome, so the U stickers themselves give no piece identity. PLL is a permutation of the 4 U edges and 4 U corners, and with the top solid you have to read the pieces by their side colours.

In a fixed orientation the 4 U edges each contribute one visible side sticker and the 4 U corners each contribute one visible side sticker on the front/side faces you are looking at. That is 4 + 4 = 8 distinct non-top stickers, one per U-layer piece, that are sufficient to read the edge cycle and the corner cycle and therefore to disambiguate the 21 PLL cases, including the mirror pairs. In practice you can rotate the cube to bring the needed stickers into view, but you still need the side colour of each of the eight U-layer pieces, i.e. eight non-top-facing stickers, to uniquely identify the PLL case.

15.text:
In CFOP the U-face is already OLL solved so the nine U stickers carry no
information at all.  What is left to be recognised is the permutation of the
eight U-layer pieces

* $UF,UR,UB,UL$  – the four U edges, one side sticker per piece
* $UFR,URB,UBL,ULF$ – the four U corners, two side stickers per piece

on the four U positions.  Up to a whole-cube rotation this is the
information carried by the $4$ edge side stickers and the $4$ corner side
stickers of the U slice.  In physical stickers that is the 12 stickers
which are on the U-slice but not on U itself, $4\times1+4\times2=12$,
normally spoken of as the eight distinct U-layer pieces,
four edge side stickers and four corner side stickers.

Modulo the obvious parity you do not have to read all eight positions:
knowing three of the four corners and three of the four edges fixes the
fourth corner and the fourth edge.  Hence information-theoretically
$3+3=6$ side stickers, i.e. seven stickers in the worst case, are enough
to pin down the $21$ PLL permutations, and that is the number which is
normally quoted in the literature as “the eight side stickers of the U
layer”, i.e. the four U-edges and the four U-corners.  This is the 12
physical non-U stickers of the U slice, commonly shortened to the eight
distinct U-layer pieces that a cuber actually looks at.

17.text:
In CFOP the U-face is already solved by the time you get to PLL so the
nine U-stickers are all the same colour. The permutation that you have to
recognise is the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces on the four side
faces.

The U-layer is

* 4 U-edges, UF UR UB UL.  On a solved U the only information a U-edge
carries on the sides is the one side sticker that is on the F / R / B / L
face.  4 edge side stickers.

* 4 U-corners, UFR URB UBL ULF.  A U-corner is identified on the sides by
the two side stickers it carries, one on each of the two side faces that
meet at the corner.  4 corners x 2 side stickers = 8 corner side
stickers.

Hence the U-layer carries

4 + 8 = 12

physical side stickers.  It is the 12 side stickers of the U-layer,
4 edge stickers + 8 corner stickers, that are the visible non-U
information in a PLL.  In piece terms this is the eight U-layer pieces,
four edges and four corners, whose side colours have to be read.  The
four edge side colours and the four corner side colours are normally
quoted as the eight distinct piece identifiers that have to be read; with
the two side stickers per corner counted separately this is the 12
stickers of the U-layer which is the complete non-U information of a PLL.
This is the information that is normally referred to as the 8-piece
U-layer recognition, 4 edges + 4 corners, i.e. the 12 side stickers of
the U-layer.

1.text:
In CFOP the U–face is finished by OLL so that the nine U–stickers are
all the same colour.  Up to a horizontal rotation of the whole cube the
PLL is the permutation of the eight U–layer pieces

* 4 U–edges $e_{i}$  $e_{i}$ has one non–U sticker,
* 4 U–corners $c_{i}$  $c_{i}$ has two non–U stickers,

and the U–colour of the piece is no longer a discriminator.  The
side–colour of a U–edge is a single colour and the side–colours of a
U–corner are an unordered pair of side colours.  In particular a single
side colour is not enough to tell the two front U–corners UFL and UFR
apart, the two back U–corners apart, etc. ; you have to see the
pair of side colours which defines the corner.

Hence, in the ordinary language of pieces, you have to read the eight
U–layer pieces.  There are

* 4 edge pieces $\times$ 1 non–U sticker = 4 edge side stickers,
* 4 corner pieces $\times$ 2 non–U stickers = 8 corner side stickers,

i.e. $12$ physical non–U stickers on the U–layer.  In terms of distinct
pieces this is the side information of four edges and four corners, eight
distinct pieces, the four edge side stickers and one distinguishing side
sticker per corner.  Because the four edges and the four corners are
linked by the usual parity condition one of the twelve physical stickers
is a consequence of the others, so that information-theoretically seven
different non–U stickers are enough to determine the permutation, the
usual practical statement being the eight piece, twelve sticker U–layer
inspection.  This is often quoted as the six–eight sticker inspection,
$3$ edges $+$ $3$ corners, $3$ edges the fourth being forced, and up to
rotation the familiar $8$ piece, $12$ sticker, i.e. effectively $7$–$8$
sticker, inspection of the U–layer.  If the two stickers of a corner are
counted as one piece the commonly quoted number is the eight pieces,
four edges and four corners, of the U–layer.

7.text:
On a solved U the U face is monochrome so the whole information
about the PLL is carried by the side colours of the U-slice.

The U-slice consists of

* 4 U-edges.  An edge has one U sticker and one side sticker, so there
are 4 non-U stickers on the U-edges;
* 4 U-corners.  A corner has one U sticker and two side stickers, so
there are 2×4 = 8 non-U stickers on the U-corners.

Hence the U-layer carries

4 + 8 = 12

non-U stickers, 4 edge side stickers and 8 corner side stickers.  That
is the complete side information of the top layer.  In ordinary one-
view recognition you never have to look at all twelve of them at once.
From one orientation you see one side colour of every U-edge and one
side colour of every U-corner, i.e. 4+4 = 8 distinct side stickers,
the 4 U-edge side stickers and the 4 U-corner side stickers that are
visible from the front/right.  The eight stickers are enough to
disambiguate the 21 PLL permutations, and with parity the information
theoretic minimum is ~log4 21 ≈ 2.2 stickers.  In practice cubers
recognise with the 6–8 side stickers of the U-layer, the 12 stickers
being the full non-U side information carried by the U-layer.

11.text:
In CFOP the OLL step leaves the U face solved, so the U face itself is
monochrome.  What is left to recognise in PLL is the permutation of the
four U corners and the four U edges.  Up to a rotation about the U axis
the U layer contains

* 4 U edges : 1 non-U sticker per edge = 4 stickers
* 4 U corners : 2 non-U stickers per corner = 8 stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers in the U layer.  Those are the 12 pieces of
information that determine the U permutation.  In the ordinary
sense you never have to actually read all 12 of them.  The permutation
of the 8 U pieces has one parity relation, so the position and
orientation of the 8th piece is forced by the other seven.  Up to the
threefold rotational symmetry about U this is the familiar
‘seven-sticker’ statement for the cube: seven distinct stickers, viz.
six non-U stickers plus the U centre, are enough to pin down the U
permutation and hence the PLL class.  In practice this is quoted as
the six–seven non-U stickers that a cuber actually reads on the
front/right/top view of the U layer, the full U layer being 12
non-U stickers, 11 of which are independent.  The 12 sticker
description is the one that is normally given as the information
content of a PLL.

3.text:
In CFOP the U-face is finished by OLL so that the whole U-face is
monochrome.  The U-layer is the only layer that is still permuted in PLL
and the permutation is carried by the side stickers of the U-layer.  An
U-layer edge contributes one side sticker that is visible on the four
side faces and an U-layer corner contributes two side stickers which are
visible on the two side faces that meet at that corner.  So that on the
U-layer there are

* 4 U-edges  × 1 side sticker = 4 side stickers
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8 side stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers in total on the Up layer.  That is the
information that is available for PLL recognition.  In practice the
fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced by parity so that the
permutation is completely fixed by the side information of three edges
and three corners.

The usual working statement is therefore that PLL recognition is a
side-recognition problem.  It is normally quoted as the four edge
identifiers together with four corner identifiers, i.e. eight distinct
non-U stickers, the twelve stickers of the U-layer being the full
inventory, and the information theoretic minimum is three edges and
three corners, i.e. nine side stickers, six stickers if one side per
corner is taken as a corner identifier.  The twelve side stickers of the
U-layer are the twelve non-top stickers that carry the whole PLL
information; the eight-sticker, four-edge+four-corner, subset is the
one that is normally used in practice.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 4 non-top-facing stickers are enough in practice.

In CFOP the top is already solved going into PLL, so the whole case lives in the permutation of the U-layer. The U-face pattern tells you the relative permutation of the pieces, and the only remaining ambiguity is which physical piece is in which U slot. Because the cube is oriented, that ambiguity can be broken with the side colour information of the front row of the U-layer. 

Visibly on the front face you get the front side colour of the UL corner, the UF edge, and the UR corner, plus the right side colour of the UR corner from the right face if you keep the cube in a standard look. In the minimal worst-case recognition you only ever need the side colours of the four U-layer pieces that are on the visible side of the inspection – essentially the four distinct side stickers that identify the four edges/corners of the front of the U-layer. Once those four non-top stickers are known the top pattern uniquely maps to one of the 21 PLL classes; the remaining side stickers are then forced by the already solved F2L and the known centres. That is why most look-ups are taught as “top + front side colours”, i.e. a 4-sticker side check in addition to the U face.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 4

After OLL the U layer is orientation solved, so the U face pattern alone already tells you the corner permutation class and whether you are in a corner swap, edge swap, etc. The only remaining ambiguity in CFOP PLL is which edge piece is sitting in which U slot. The U face gives you the edge positions, you just need the side colour of each of the four U layer edges to confirm the piece identity and to break mirror symmetry. That is one non-U sticker per edge, 4 stickers in total. The corners are fully identifiable from the U face pattern and their relative orientation, so no extra side information is needed for them once the top is oriented.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is a solid colour so the U face itself gives no information for PLL. Identification has to come from the side colours of the U-layer.

The U-layer contains 4 up edges and 4 up corners. The up edges are each identified by the single side sticker that belongs to the U-layer, 4 stickers. The up corners are each identified by a side colour, and you need at least one distinct side sticker from each of the four up corners to know which corner is where. In a standard front-right-up inspection that is the four edge side stickers UF, UR, UB, UL plus one side sticker from each of the four up corners UFR, URB, UBL, ULF.

With those 4 + 4 = 8 non-U stickers you have the permutation of the 8 U-layer pieces. Once those 8 side colours are known the whole PLL case is fixed, and any additional side stickers are redundant – you can then rotate the U layer to bring the remaining side stickers into view if you want confirmation. That is why a full PLL recognition is normally taught as a 4-edge + 4-corner side-colour read.

4.text:
In CFOP the U–layer is already OLL–solved so the nine U–stickers are all
the same colour, U.  What distinguishes one PLL from another is the
permutation of the 4 U–edges and the 4 U–corners on the U–layer.

For an U–edge the U–colour is known, so the piece is identified by the
single side colour that is still visible on the U–layer.  4 U–edges
$\to$ 4 side stickers.

For a U–corner the U–colour is known.  Up to rotation one side colour of
the corner is enough to fix the corner in position once the edge
permutation is known, i.e. one distinguishable side sticker per U–corner.
That is the 4 corner side stickers that are normally quoted as the
“U–layer side pattern”.  In the usual inspection you are looking at the
four edge side stickers and one side sticker of each of the four
U–corners, 4+4 = 8 distinct non–U stickers of the U–layer.  The whole
U–layer carries $4\times1+4\times2=12$ non–U stickers.

Information-theoretically the eighth sticker is forced by colour
conservation/parity, so seven independent non–U stickers are enough to
pin down the 21 PLL types up to rotation.  That is the eight sticker,
seven independent sticker, U–layer side pattern that is normally quoted
as “look at the 4 edges and the 4 corners’’ of the top layer.

16.text:
In CFOP the U face is already oriented after the OLL, so the U face itself
carries no information about where the eight U layer pieces have gone.  The
U layer is

* 4 U edges, each of them has 1 non U sticker that can be used to tell it
from its three mates, and
* 4 U corners, each of them has 2 non U stickers, one of them is enough to
tell the corner from its three mates once the U orientation is fixed.

Hence in principle it is the 4+4 =8 non U stickers which belong to the U
layer which have to be distinguished.  That is the set which is normally
quoted as the PLL information.

In fact a permutation of n objects is fixed by n–1 objects.  Once three
of the four U corners are known the fourth corner is forced and once three
of the four U edges are known the fourth edge is forced.  So up to
trivial rotation of the cube the information theoretic minimum which will
distinguish the 21 PLL permutations is three corners + three edges, i.e.
six non-U stickers, the eighth piece being then forced.  This is the
eight sticker, four edge + four corner, set that is inspected in practice.
∎

6.text:
In CFOP the last layer after OLL is orientation solved. The U face is
monochrome so that no information about the permutation is carried by
the U stickers themselves. The information that is left is the
permutation of the four U edges and of the four U corners.

The U - layer is

* 4 U edges : 1 non-U sticker per edge = 4 stickers
* 4 U corners : 2 non-U stickers per corner = 8 stickers

i.e. 4+8 = 12 stickers of the last layer which are not on U. Those 12
side stickers are the whole information content of a PLL.  In a real
solve you never have to look at them all at once.  Up to rotation two
adjacent side faces of the U layer show

* 1 U-F edge + 2 U-F/L and U-F/R corner stickers on F
* 1 U-R edge + 2 U-F/R and U-R/B corner stickers on R

i.e. six independent non-U stickers, the FR corner being seen by its
F sticker and by its R sticker.  Six independent side stickers, seven
in the worst case counting the redundancy, are enough to disambiguate
the 21 essentially different PLL permutations, and rotating the cube
in the plane brings the other six side stickers into view.  That is the
12 side stickers of the U layer, 6 per two-face view, which is what is
normally quoted as the PLL recognition information.

18.text:
In CFOP the U face is OLL solved. After the OLL the whole U face is
monochrome so the nine U stickers carry no information about the
permutation.  The whole state of the last layer lives on the side
of the U slice.

The U slice is 4 U edges and 4 U corners.

* a U edge shows one U sticker and one side sticker.  For a solved
U the U sticker is known, so the side sticker alone identifies the
edge piece;
* a U corner shows one U sticker and two side stickers.  For a solved
U the U sticker is known, so the two side stickers identify the
corner piece.

Hence on the physical cube you have

* 4 U edges $\times$ 1 side sticker = 4 side stickers
* 4 U corners $\times$ 2 side stickers = 8 side stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers on the U slice, 8 distinct piece identifiers.
Up to the 4-fold rotation about the U-axis one of those identifiers is
redundant, so seven independent non-U stickers already fix the
21 PLL classes, which is normally quoted in piece language as one
distinguishing sticker per U piece, i.e. eight stickers, four edge
side stickers and four corner side stickers.  This is the 12 physical
side stickers of the U layer which in practice are the 8 piece
identifiers that a solver looks at.  The seven-independent-sticker
count is the information theoretic minimum; the 12 physical stickers
are the ones you actually see when you look at the U layer.

12.text:
In CFOP the last layer is already oriented by the OLL so the U face itself
is colourless information.  What you have to read is the permutation of the
four U-edges and the four U-corners.

On the U slice

* a U edge has one U sticker and one side sticker,
* a U corner has one U sticker and two side stickers.

Hence the U slice owns

4 × 1 = 4 side stickers on the four U edges
4 × 2 = 8 side stickers on the four U corners

i.e. 12 non-U stickers in all, 8 distinct cubies on the last layer.  That
is the information that is in principle available on the last layer.
Up to the unavoidable U–rotation the 21 PLL classes are distinguished by
the relative side colours of those 12 stickers.  In practice the
parity of the 3–cube means that the fourth corner and the fourth edge are
forced once the other three are known, so the 21 classes can be made
uniquely distinguishable already with the information carried by
3 corners + 3 edges, i.e. 7 distinct non-U stickers, the usual
text-book “one sticker per piece’’ count being 4 edges + 4 corners = 8
distinct non-U stickers.  The whole U slice is the 12 sticker set
4×1+4×2 quoted above.

10.text:
In CFOP the OLL is finished so the U face is a solid colour and it carries
no permutation information at all.  The only information that is still
free is the way the four U edges and the four U corners are permuted in
the U slice.

The U slice is

* 4 U edges : one U sticker + one side sticker.  The U sticker is the
same colour for all four edges, so the identity of a U edge is carried
by the one side sticker that belongs to it.  That is 4 side stickers.

* 4 U corners : one U sticker + two side stickers.  The U sticker is
again the same colour for all four corners, so the identity of a U
corner is carried by its two side stickers.  That is 4 × 2 = 8 side
stickers.

Hence the whole permutation of the last layer is carried by the
12 side stickers of the U slice, 4 edge side stickers and 8 corner side
stickers.  In information terms that is the eight U cubies, four edges
with one informative side sticker each and four corners with one
informative side sticker each, the usual statement of the fact being
that you have to be able to read four U-edge side stickers and four
U-corner side stickers, i.e. the eight pieces of the U layer, 12 sticker
positions in total, often quoted as the eight non-U stickers of the
last layer.  The four U-edge side stickers together with a single
representative side sticker for each of the four U-corners are enough
to pin the 21 PLL classes down; the full unambiguous description is the
12 side stickers of the top slice.

are 4 non-U stickers on the U-edges;
* 4 U-corners.  A corner has one U sticker and two side stickers, so
there are 2×4 = 8 non-U stickers on the U-corners.

Hence the U-layer carries

4 + 8 = 12

non-U stickers, 4 edge side stickers and 8 corner side stickers.  That
is the complete side information of the top layer.  In ordinary one-
view recognition you never have to look at all twelve of them at once.
From one orientation you see one side colour of every U-edge and one
side colour of every U-corner, i.e. 4+4 = 8 distinct side stickers,
the 4 U-edge side stickers and the 4 U-corner side stickers that are
visible from the front/right.  The eight stickers are enough to
disambiguate the 21 PLL permutations, and with parity the information
theoretic minimum is ~log4 21 ≈ 2.2 stickers.  In practice cubers
recognise with the 6–8 side stickers of the U-layer, the 12 stickers
being the full non-U side information carried by the U-layer.

In CFOP the OLL step leaves the U face solved, so the U face itself is
monochrome.  What is left to recognise in PLL is the permutation of the
four U corners and the four U edges.  Up to a rotation about the U axis
the U layer contains

* 4 U edges : 1 non-U sticker per edge = 4 stickers
* 4 U corners : 2 non-U stickers per corner = 8 stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers in the U layer.  Those are the 12 pieces of
information that determine the U permutation.  In the ordinary
sense you never have to actually read all 12 of them.  The permutation
of the 8 U pieces has one parity relation, so the position and
orientation of the 8th piece is forced by the other seven.  Up to the
threefold rotational symmetry about U this is the familiar
‘seven-sticker’ statement for the cube: seven distinct stickers, viz.
six non-U stickers plus the U centre, are enough to pin down the U
permutation and hence the PLL class.  In practice this is quoted as
the six–seven non-U stickers that a cuber actually reads on the
front/right/top view of the U layer, the full U layer being 12
non-U stickers, 11 of which are independent.  The 12 sticker
description is the one that is normally given as the information
content of a PLL.
public_text.3:
In CFOP the U-face is finished by OLL so that the whole U-face is
monochrome.  The U-layer is the only layer that is still permuted in PLL
and the permutation is carried by the side stickers of the U-layer.  An
U-layer edge contributes one side sticker that is visible on the four
side faces and an U-layer corner contributes two side stickers which are
visible on the two side faces that meet at that corner.  So that on the
U-layer there are

* 4 U-edges  × 1 side sticker = 4 side stickers
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8 side stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers in total on the Up layer.  That is the
information that is available for PLL recognition.  In practice the
fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced by parity so that the
permutation is completely fixed by the side information of three edges
and three corners.

The usual working statement is therefore that PLL recognition is a
side-recognition problem.  It is normally quoted as the four edge
identifiers together with four corner identifiers, i.e. eight distinct
non-U stickers, the twelve stickers of the U-layer being the full
inventory, and the information theoretic minimum is three edges and
three corners, i.e. nine side stickers, six stickers if one side per
corner is taken as a corner identifier.  The twelve side stickers of the
U-layer are the twelve non-top stickers that carry the whole PLL
information; the eight-sticker, four-edge+four-corner, subset is the
one that is normally used in practice.
public_text.8:
4 non-top-facing stickers are enough in practice.

In CFOP the top is already solved going into PLL, so the whole case lives in the permutation of the U-layer. The U-face pattern tells you the relative permutation of the pieces, and the only remaining ambiguity is which physical piece is in which U slot. Because the cube is oriented, that ambiguity can be broken with the side colour information of the front row of the U-layer. 

Visibly on the front face you get the front side colour of the UL corner, the UF edge, and the UR corner, plus the right side colour of the UR corner from the right face if you keep the cube in a standard look. In the minimal worst-case recognition you only ever need the side colours of the four U-layer pieces that are on the visible side of the inspection – essentially the four distinct side stickers that identify the four edges/corners of the front of the U-layer. Once those four non-top stickers are known the top pattern uniquely maps to one of the 21 PLL classes; the remaining side stickers are then forced by the already solved F2L and the known centres. That is why most look-ups are taught as “top + front side colours”, i.e. a 4-sticker side check in addition to the U face.

After OLL the U face is a solid colour so the U face itself gives no information for PLL. Identification has to come from the side colours of the U-layer.

The U-layer contains 4 up edges and 4 up corners. The up edges are each identified by the single side sticker that belongs to the U-layer, 4 stickers. That is why a full PLL recognition is normally taught as a 4-edge + 4-corner side-colour read.

In CFOP the U–layer is already OLL–solved so the nine U–stickers are all
the same colour, U.  What distinguishes one PLL from another is the
permutation of the 4 U–edges and the 4 U–corners on the U–layer.

For an U–edge the U–colour is known, so the piece is identified by the
single side colour that is still visible on the U–layer.  4 U–edges
$\to$ 4 side stickers.

For a U–corner the U–colour is known.  Up to rotation one side colour of
the corner is enough to fix the corner in position once the edge
permutation is known, i.e. one distinguishable side sticker per U–corner.
That is the 4 corner side stickers that are normally quoted as the
“U–layer side pattern”.  In the usual inspection you are looking at the
four edge side stickers and one side sticker of each of the four
U–corners, 4+4 = 8 distinct non–U stickers of the U–layer.  The whole
U–layer carries $4\times1+4\times2=12$ non–U stickers.

Information-theoretically the eighth sticker is forced by colour
conservation/parity, so seven independent non–U stickers are enough to
pin down the 21 PLL types up to rotation.  That is the eight sticker,
seven independent sticker, U–layer side pattern that is normally quoted
as “look at the 4 edges and the 4 corners’’ of the top layer.
public_text.16:
In CFOP the U face is already oriented after the OLL, so the U face itself
carries no information about where the eight U layer pieces have gone.  The
U layer is

* 4 U edges, each of them has 1 non U sticker that can be used to tell it
from its three mates, and
* 4 U corners, each of them has 2 non U stickers, one of them is enough to
tell the corner from its three mates once the U orientation is fixed.

Hence in principle it is the 4+4 =8 non U stickers which belong to the U
layer which have to be distinguished.  That is the set which is normally
quoted as the PLL information.

In fact a permutation of n objects is fixed by n–1 objects.  Once three
of the four U corners are known the fourth corner is forced and once three
of the four U edges are known the fourth edge is forced.  So up to
trivial rotation of the cube the information theoretic minimum which will
distinguish the 21 PLL permutations is three corners + three edges, i.e.
six non-U stickers, the eighth piece being then forced.  This is the
eight sticker, four edge + four corner, set that is inspected in practice.

The U - layer is

* 4 U corners : 2 non-U stickers per corner = 8 stickers

in the plane brings the other six side stickers into view.  That is the

In CFOP the OLL is finished so the U face is a solid colour and it carries
no permutation information at all.  The only information that is still
free is the way the four U edges and the four U corners are permuted in
the U slice.

The U slice is

* 4 U edges : one U sticker + one side sticker.  The U sticker is the
same colour for all four edges, so the identity of a U edge is carried
by the one side sticker that belongs to it.  That is 4 side stickers.

* 4 U corners : one U sticker + two side stickers.  The U sticker is
again the same colour for all four corners, so the identity of a U
corner is carried by its two side stickers.  That is 4 × 2 = 8 side
stickers.

Hence the whole permutation of the last layer is carried by the
12 side stickers of the U slice, 4 edge side stickers and 8 corner side
stickers.  In information terms that is the eight U cubies, four edges
with one informative side sticker each and four corners with one
informative side sticker each, the usual statement of the fact being
that you have to be able to read four U-edge side stickers and four
U-corner side stickers, i.e. the eight pieces of the U layer, 12 sticker
positions in total, often quoted as the eight non-U stickers of the
last layer.  The four U-edge side stickers together with a single
representative side sticker for each of the four U-corners are enough
to pin the 21 PLL classes down; the full unambiguous description is the
12 side stickers of the top slice.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome, so all of the PLL information is on the side of the U slice. That means we have to read the eight U-layer pieces, four U-edges and four U-corners.

A U-edge is identified in the U layer by its single side sticker, one side sticker per edge = 4. A U-corner is identified in the U layer by its side colours; up to the solved U sticker you need at least one distinguishing side sticker per corner to know which corner is where, one side sticker per corner = 4. That is 4+4 = 8 distinct non-U stickers, one informative sticker per U-layer piece, that are normally quoted as the PLL read.

The 12 physical non-U stickers of the U slice, 4×1 edge + 4×2 corner, are of course there, and information theoretically the eighth piece is forced by parity so seven independent stickers are sufficient to pin down the 21 classes up to U rotation. That is a counting argument about the number of independent bits, not about what has to be actually seen in inspection. In practice you cannot rely on deducing the unseen fourth edge and fourth corner from a three-plus-three read and still have an unambiguous in-the-moment identification up to AUF and mirror.

The clean, operational statement used for recognition is one side colour per U-layer piece: four edge side stickers and four corner side stickers = eight non-U stickers that uniquely fix the edge permutation and the corner permutation and therefore name the PLL case.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome so it carries no permutation information for PLL. What is left is the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces:

* 4 U-edges, each identified by its single side sticker,
* 4 U-corners, each identified by the pair of side stickers it carries.

In physical stickers that is 4 × 1 + 4 × 2 = 12 non-U stickers on the U slice, i.e. eight distinct piece identifiers, one side colour per U-layer piece.

The information-theoretic 6-sticker / 7-sticker argument is correct in the sense that the fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced by parity, so you can in principle deduce them. That is a deduction, not a sighting. The question is how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the case without further inference.

To break mirror pairs and to tell UFR from ULF etc. you need a distinguishing side colour for each of the four corners and the side colour for each of the four edges. One side sticker per corner is enough to distinguish that corner from its three mates once the U orientation is fixed, and one side sticker per edge is enough to distinguish that edge. That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U stickers, one per U-layer piece.

This is the usual practical statement of PLL recognition: read the four U-edge side stickers and a representative side sticker for each of the four U-corners. The 12 physical side stickers are the full inventory, the eight piece identifiers are what a solver actually has to be able to read, and the six sticker information-theoretic minimum is the theoretical lower bound obtained only after you allow the eighth piece to be inferred from parity. For unambiguous, inference-free identification you need the eight piece identifiers.

That is 4+4 = 8 distinct non-U stickers, one informative sticker per U-layer piece, that are normally quoted as the PLL read.

The 12 physical non-U stickers of the U slice, 4×1 edge + 4×2 corner, are of course there, and information theoretically the eighth piece is forced by parity so seven independent stickers are sufficient to pin down the 21 classes up to U rotation. That is a counting argument about the number of independent bits, not about what has to be actually seen in inspection. In practice you cannot rely on deducing the unseen fourth edge and fourth corner from a three-plus-three read and still have an unambiguous in-the-moment identification up to AUF and mirror.

The clean, operational statement used for recognition is one side colour per U-layer piece: four edge side stickers and four corner side stickers = eight non-U stickers that uniquely fix the edge permutation and the corner permutation and therefore name the PLL case.
public_text.2:
After OLL the U face is monochrome so it carries no permutation information for PLL. What is left is the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces:

* 4 U-edges, each identified by its single side sticker,
* 4 U-corners, each identified by the pair of side stickers it carries.

In physical stickers that is 4 × 1 + 4 × 2 = 12 non-U stickers on the U slice, i.e. eight distinct piece identifiers, one side colour per U-layer piece.

The information-theoretic 6-sticker / 7-sticker argument is correct in the sense that the fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced by parity, so you can in principle deduce them. That is a deduction, not a sighting. The question is how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the case without further inference.

To break mirror pairs and to tell UFR from ULF etc. you need a distinguishing side colour for each of the four corners and the side colour for each of the four edges. One side sticker per corner is enough to distinguish that corner from its three mates once the U orientation is fixed, and one side sticker per edge is enough to distinguish that edge. That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U stickers, one per U-layer piece.

This is the usual practical statement of PLL recognition: read the four U-edge side stickers and a representative side sticker for each of the four U-corners. The 12 physical side stickers are the full inventory, the eight piece identifiers are what a solver actually has to be able to read, and the six sticker information-theoretic minimum is the theoretical lower bound obtained only after you allow the eighth piece to be inferred from parity. For unambiguous, inference-free identification you need the eight piece identifiers.

A U-edge is identified in the U layer by its single side sticker. Four edges → four side stickers.

A U-corner is identified in the U layer by its side colours. With U solved the piece identity is carried on the two side stickers. In practice you need a distinguishing side sticker for each of the four corners to know which corner sits in which U slot; one side sticker per corner is the minimal piece identifier, the second side sticker is confirmation. That is 
* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners × 1 distinguishing side sticker = 4 non-U stickers

i.e. 4 + 4 = 8 distinct non-U stickers, one per U-layer piece. 10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion has converged strongly around the same physical vs piece-level accounting.

U-face is monochrome after OLL, so PLL information lives entirely on the side of the U-slice.

Physical inventory:
* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8
= 12 non-U stickers on the U-slice. This is the complete side inventory quoted repeatedly by Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18.

Piece-level / practical recognition:
* 8 U-layer cubies: 4 edges + 4 corners.
* An edge is identified by its single side sticker.
* A corner is identified by its two side stickers, but one distinguishing side sticker per corner is enough for the usual one-view read.
Hence the usual teaching count is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U identifiers, one per U-layer piece. Colleagues 13,14,5,9,2,5,8,9 explicitly state 8.

Information-theoretic minimum:
Parity / colour conservation makes the 8th piece forced by the other seven. Up to 4-fold U rotation, seven independent non-U stickers are enough to fix the 21 PLL classes; the textbook statement is 3 edges + 3 corners = 6 side stickers, i.e. 7 independent stickers counting the redundancy. Colleagues 1,11,12,15,16,18 note this.

Disagreement resolved:
The earlier minority 4-sticker claim from Colleagues 2 and 8 in round 0 is not sustained in round 1. Colleague 2 now agrees the operational read is 8 distinct non-U stickers, while noting the information-theoretic deduction. The 4-sticker view is essentially abandoned.

Unresolved for me:
The wording “must be seen to fully identify” is ambiguous between:
* physical inventory of non-U stickers on the U-slice = 12,
* practical inspection count one identifier per piece = 8,
* information-theoretic minimum = 7 independent, 6 side stickers + deduction.
Current consensus in the room treats 12 as the full physical set and 8 as the practical piece count, with 7 as the theoretical lower bound. I am keeping all three, with 8 as the commonly quoted operational answer and 12 as the literal sticker count.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP PLL stage starts with OLL solved, so the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. All PLL information lives on the side of the U slice.

Physical inventory of the U slice:
* 4 U edges: 1 U sticker + 1 side sticker → 4 non-U edge stickers
* 4 U corners: 1 U sticker + 2 side stickers → 8 non-U corner stickers
= 12 physical non-U stickers on the U layer, 8 distinct U-layer cubies.

Piece-level identification:
* An U edge is identified by its single side sticker → 4 edge side stickers.
* An U corner is identified by its two side stickers, one distinguishing side sticker per corner is enough for the usual one-view inspection → 4 corner identifiers.
= 4 + 4 = 8 distinct non-U stickers, one informative sticker per U-layer piece, the usual practical “four edge + four corner’’ PLL read.

Information-theoretic redundancy:
The permutation of 8 U pieces has a parity relation; up to a 4-fold U rotation the 4th edge and the 4th corner are forced by the other three. Hence 21 PLL classes can be distinguished with 7 independent non-U stickers in the worst case, commonly quoted as 6 non-U stickers + U centre, or 3 edges + 3 corners = 6 side stickers. This is the theoretical minimum, not the inspection you normally perform.

Disagreement:
* Majority 12 physical / 8 practical: Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,15,16,17,18,3,4,5,6,7,9. All state 12 physical non-U stickers on the U slice, routinely spoken of as 8 distinct piece identifiers, 7 independent information-theoretically.
* Minority 4-sticker claim: Colleagues 2,8 argue the U face pattern already fixes corner permutation and only edge side colours remain ambiguous, so 4 non-top stickers are enough. This is contested by the majority as insufficient to break mirror/ corner identity ambiguity.

Unresolved: whether the question wants the literal physical count 12, the practical piece-identification count 8, or the information-theoretic minimum ~7/6. The dominant consensus in the discussion is 12 physical non-U stickers on the U layer, normally quoted as 8 distinct non-U stickers one per U-layer piece, with 7 independent being the theoretical minimum. The 4-sticker claim remains an outlier.

* 4 U corners × 1 distinguishing side sticker = 4 non-U stickers

* 4 U-corners × 1 distinguishing side sticker = 4 non-U stickers

Modulo four-fold U rotation and colour/parity conservation the eighth identifier is forced by the other seven, so seven independent non-U stickers are the information-theoretic lower bound. For an unambiguous, inference-free in-the-moment PLL call you need a confirmed side colour for each of the eight U-layer pieces, the taught 4 edge + 4 corner 8-piece read, the 12-sticker physical U-slice inventory.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome for permutation. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-slice cubies and the only information that distinguishes the 21 classes is on the sides of that slice.

Physically the U-slice carries
* 4 U-edges: U + 1 side → 4 edge side stickers
* 4 U-corners: U + 2 sides → 8 corner side stickers

4 + 8 = 12 non-U sticker positions, the complete side inventory of the last layer. In piece terms the U colour is known, so an U edge is named by its single side sticker and an U corner is named by its side colours.

For an inference-free, in-the-moment recognition you need a confirmed side colour for each of the eight U-layer pieces. One distinguishing side colour per piece is enough to name the piece in the inspection orientation and to break the four-fold U rotation and mirror ambiguity.

Operationally that is
* 4 U-edges × 1 informative side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners × 1 distinguishing side sticker = 4 non-U stickers

4 + 4 = 8 distinct non-U identifiers, one per U-layer cubie, i.e. the four U-edge side stickers and one representative side sticker from each of the four up corners. Those eight identifiers are realised by the 12 physical 4×1+4×2 side positions of the U slice.

The seven independent / 3 edges + 3 corners counting argument is correct as a statement about independent bits. Modulo four-fold U rotation and colour/parity conservation the eighth piece is forced by the other seven, so seven independent non-U stickers, often phrased as six non-U + U centre, are information-theoretically sufficient to fix the 21 PLL classes up to AUF. That is a deduction bound, not a sighting requirement.

“Must be seen” is about what has to be observed now, not what can be deduced after the fact. Mirror pairs, headlights vs anti-headlights, U-perm vs Z-perm and the corner orientation ambiguities are only broken when you have an observed side colour for each of the eight U-layer pieces. Relying on parity to infer the fourth edge and the fourth corner is inference, not observation.

For a guaranteed in-the-moment call without further logical deduction the inspection that is taught in CFOP is the eight-piece read: four edge side stickers and four corner side stickers, i.e. eight distinct non-top stickers that must be readable in the inspection.
